utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we first hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And today's appearances, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, Your Honour, Kapila Waidyaratne with Mr. Nicholas Koumjian, and Ruth Karper. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the complete Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, good morning. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before starting, several issues. First of all, Ms. Karper, my apologies, because indeed, it's correct, the document I needed was at least in my sphere and it was my fault to rely only on the short summary of the OTP, indeed, misleading to that answer that we regarded the witness as necessary to hear as a live witness. Sorry about this. Secondly, you may have heard by rumours on the corridor or somewhere else that there was a Status Conference held last Friday in this case office of the Prosecutor versus Mr. Mrdja. In the framework of this Status Conference, there was a discussion when the case versus Mr. Mrdja should be heard. You may know that it's a relatively new indictment and Mr. Mrdja was just recently arrested. Ex officio, the Trial Chamber came to the conclusion that normally, the prerequisites of Rule 48, joinder of accused, would be met but we didn't go in any discussion of this point because we believe such a joinder would infringe both the rights of Dr. Stakic and Dr. Mrdja. Nevertheless, we have to take care that all cases be heard expeditiously. Therefore, it was discussed during this Status Conference whether or not it could be possible to hear the case versus Mrdja during the break in the Stakic case, bearing in mind that it was in the beginning a request from this Defence to have a break of about three months. It was discussed there that the Prosecutor's case would take, realistically, maximum period of four weeks only and, therefore, it could be feasible. No doubt, we have other problems to face, such as: Courtroom availability; does it really fit into our programme; does the Secretary-General of the United Nations assign the same Bench for this case, and so on and so forth. But I regard it as necessary to inform you already today on what's planned. Any comments from the parties as regards this latter point?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have no special comments, Your Honour, but we are ready to take a longer break than is scheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I understand that you are not interested to try to have a joinder.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We would prefer to have a separate trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We thought this, and I think it's indeed adequate. From the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nothing to add this morning. I think, Your Honour, the way we left it, I don't know if Mr. Lukic and the Defence know this, but both parties were asked to submit in writing their views about being able to start on the 1st of October and for the Mrdja case, and we haven't done that but we're going to do that in writing. There are some issues we have to deal with, principally Rule 68, and how long it will take to do the necessary search for Rule 68. Other than that, I don't have any other issues except to say that I think the Defence shouldn't count on it yet because it's not yet completely resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. As I mentioned before, there are numerous possible obstacles, but it shouldn't be the case that you hear probably even misleading rumours, be it in the Detention Unit or be it on the corridors of this premises. So, therefore, this observation. But as regards Mrdja, I really want to invite Mr. Koumjian, if there is any problem, let us know immediately because it seems to be absolutely necessary to use all the possible dates to hear the case. Otherwise, it could be somewhere in 2005, if not 2006, which is not a realistic perspective. Ms. Korner, last Thursday, before discussing the one or other issue, she told us that you, Mr. Koumjian, would address us with a problem as regards the signatures. Is there still a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, there is. But perhaps I could do it -- I may have some more information this morning, and I would rather wait until I have all the information before I speak to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then finally, we got the Prosecution's fourth notice for admission of transcripts and videos pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Is the Defence already prepared to respond to this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. If it's the fifth notice for admission of transcript pursuant to Rule 92 bis, I'm prepared. If it's the fourth one, I'm not prepared actually to discuss that because I'm not sure what videos the Court is referring to. I only received this morning the Prosecution's fifth notice for admission of transcript involving a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are always better treated by the OTP and Registry than the Judges. We don't have this yet, but probably nevertheless you can give your commentaries to the transcript already now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to the Prosecutor's fifth notice, we object, Your Honour, and ask that this witness be presented live, although we understand his medical condition. And the basis for which we believe that he shall be presented live is as follows: Initially, this witness was brought to the Tribunal. They cite the same reasons that they cited in the prior case, the Tadic case, i.e., some hearing impairment that the witness has sustained. That didn't seem to be a problem in the testimony that the witness gave in the Tadic trial. And it seemed that the witness, although the cross-examination was extremely limited, was able to endure even cross-examination questions by both the Defence counsel as well as the panel of Judges who were present. We believe that our rights to confront and to cross-examine a witness is imperative, and that although we have at times stipulated to 92 bis witnesses, this witness does touch upon various issues that are critical and important to the Defence and also to specific elements in the fourth amended revised indictment. For those reasons, we ask that the witness be brought in or that the OTP present another witness who would have, as they have in the past, experienced parallel views and experiences within that time period at issue. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Arguments in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, admittedly our information regarding the condition comes from -- mainly from the spouse of the witness. And I'm unsure if the investigator actually was able to speak to the witness. Perhaps once. I think he was having a lot of trouble speaking to the witness. But even if the witness, even if we presume the witness had no problem, medical problem, that still would not necessarily mean the witness is not appropriate for 92 bis. The question is what in the witness's statement is it that the Defence feels is not appropriate for 92 bis, or would make it worth the time to have the witness brought here live to testify. I think, as I recall, this is a pure crime-base witness, and we think it's appropriate for 92 bis for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll decide on this as soon as possible. And as time is of the essence and we have to decide on all these issues, no doubt before the Court recess, I would ask the Defence to comment on the fourth notice for admission of transcripts and videos pursuant to Rule 92 bis, if possible, before the -- immediately after the second break of today, if you could take it. Anything in addition? I can't see anything. Therefore, would the witness of today, which is number -- we have two possibilities. Please let us know what's the number of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Number 27, Your Honour, according to 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 27. And this witness will be heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: As requested, protective measures, Your Honour, of pseudonym and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Pseudonym, image distortion. And pseudonym would be now, please, "W"? Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: "U." Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "U." Okay. Then Witness U, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, is it envisaged that we can conclude the witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the witness for tomorrow is prepared as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you hear in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's hear the solemn declaration of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Please understand that we will call you "Witness U" only, and not with your last name. This is for the purpose of your own protection. And so please don't regard it as an uncourtesy. So, please, the OTP may start the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I at the beginning request to Your Honour to go into private session as I would be leading some personal information with regard to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, talking about Kamicani, could you tell us very briefly the distances between Kamicani and Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 13 and 14 kilometres, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And when you go to Prijedor from Kamicani, you pass the town called Kozarac. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you pass beside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What about Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you pass by Kozarusa again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was the distance between Kamicani and Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my -- about 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was the majority of the population in Kamicani, from what you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims were predominant, that is, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Roughly, approximately, did you know what the population was in majority, the Muslim population in Kamicani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about 90 per cent. It was the predominant group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was there a mosque in Kamicani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mosque was, when you arrived from Kozarac, about -- at one kilometre from Kozarac, and then about a kilometre from the local commune building. So it was midway between the two, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness U, when did you stop work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A week before the attack on Kozarac, that is, on Kamicani.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you say that, when was Kamicani attacked, according to what you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, around 2.00. No, actually, it was on the 24th of May, and the 26th was the day when the attack finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So you stopped work one week before the 24th of May, 1992. What made you stop work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't able to move about and go off to my business in Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Why do you say that you were unable to move about? Could you explain as to what happened or what was the obstruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Following the takeover by Serb authorities in Prijedor Municipality, during that last period, there were security measures and control measures and checkpoints that had been introduced. So at some point, you couldn't just pass through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you say that there were security measures and control measures and checkpoints. Were they manned by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that Kamicani was attacked and shelled on the 24th of May, 1992. Do you recall before that any negotiations or any discussions that took place of what you heard and knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you explain what happened and when this happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I actually attended, after I had found out from my neighbours that people were arriving who had taken part in negotiations in Prijedor following the takeover of Prijedor Municipality by Serb authorities, which meant that a group of people had been elected from the Kozarac region, had been selected to go and negotiate with these new authorities, the newly self-imposed authorities. So a group of people were selected to go there and discuss this newly arisen situation with the new authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did they come back and say what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They arrived there at the Kamicani local commune building. Probably, they went about other local communes, too. And they talked about their discussions with the authorities in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What did you hear from them, and who was the person who said this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know exactly the number of persons in that group of negotiators, but Dr. Jusuf Pasic was among them, Asim Fazlic also. These two persons I knew. And in that group, there may have been other people, but not that I knew, or at least on that particular day, I didn't see any other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was there any demands from the Serb authorities of what these speakers or the people who came back told you all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I understood, that was at least what I understood back then or that's what Jusuf Pasic said literally. He talked about the negotiations and what the subject of the negotiations had been. However, the room was packed with people and everyone was listening. So Jusuf Pasic, perhaps, simplified the matter a bit, and this is literally what he said. He said: "As negotiators" - and I am referring to the group who had gone to Prijedor to negotiate - "we are in an unequal position as a negotiating team to negotiate our terms, and you must be aware of that." He was referring to us who were listening. "They" - and I am here referring to the Prijedor municipal authorities - "are the occupation force." That's what he said. "And they tell us what to do. And they are not asking us what we thought was to be done. They were not requesting our proposals. This is something you must understand. That's what the situation is like," he said. And we ended on that note, on that piece of information. Whether there were any further negotiating teams later on, whether contact was established with the authorities in Prijedor, I couldn't tell. But probably the result of those negotiations was precisely the attack of the Serb forces on the 24th and 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was there any mention of handing over of weapons and being loyal to the Serb authorities? Was there anything of that nature mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the things discussed. They requested the TO, the reserve forces of the Territorial Defence of the former Yugoslavia, of the former Yugoslav army, active in the Kozarac, they requested that they turn in their weapons and that both active and reserve police forces should return their weapons so that the new Serb authorities could occupy the police station and fill the remaining posts, official positions, in the Kozarac area. What followed from that was that Muslim police officers were not to possess any weapons and were not to continue their daily duties as policemen. And that was then the end to their activity. And what would have followed afterwards, we can only speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did you have any weapons with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, after these discussions or the matter that you referred earlier, what happened on the 24th of May, 1992, and where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 24th, it was a Sunday, roughly at 2.00 in the afternoon. I happened to be in the area of Kamicani or, more specifically, in the hamlet of Forici, thereabouts. I talked to one of the locals there at the entrance to the hamlet, and suddenly there were shots and very loud explosions. I didn't know which direction it was coming from at that moment, but I know that there were powerful detonations while I was there before I ran off to hide, and there was rubble flying through the air. So at that moment, I took shelter in a garage nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any other explosions or shells hit the targets while you were in the garage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From the moment it began, that was the first moment of the attack, it went on for some time. So from the garage in which I was staying, there was no front door there. As far as I could see, I saw where the shells were falling, falling on the houses and all over the place, with loud explosions. So it was probably also due to the fear I felt because that was the first time I saw anything like that happening. Probably, I even consciously refrained from watching. But then again, I was not in a position to see clearly what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any houses be damaged by such shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the houses across the way from where I was, and then 200 metres down the road, I saw a shell land on one roof and the house just fell apart and the roof started burning. And I didn't see how that ended up, what happened to the house, but I saw the shell fall on the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you were in this garage, were wounded brought to that place, a wounded man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From the moment I came to the garage, there arrived some other locals, men and women from the area, and they stayed with me there. And we didn't leave the garage for at least between one and two hours. And some three young men were there, and then some elderly locals also. And then some were in a different place, I'm not sure, further down or further up the street. And then a wounded man was brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see as to what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were passing by that garage where I was staying and they saw probably that there were people inside there, so they brought him there for us to help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you and any other person take this wounded man to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to provide whatever assistance we could, but none of us were trained medical staff. And we were scared, too, and ignorant as to what we were supposed to do. So our first idea was to take the man to hospital in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you take that wounded person to Kozarac, the hospital in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: With whom did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next to the garage there, I mean, there were other people in the garage, a number of locals. So next to the garage, there was a lorry driven by one of the neighbours. So we put the wounded man on to the lorry and we kept him in the back of the lorry, and that's how we continued on for Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: On your way to Kozarac, did you see, observe, any houses on the way, damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On my way, I was sitting in the back with the wounded man. It was a rather small lorry, with the canvas lowered. But it flapped in the wind so every now and then, as I was holding the wounded man in my lap, I could see electricity posts torn down by shells, and I could see shell-pimpled houses. I could see tree trunks lying all over the road, probably also hit by shells, that sort of thing. So that was along the road to the hospital. That was the situation. I did not watch all the time, but when the canvas was pulled up by the wind, I could see the situation outside along the road. I did not watch consistently during the whole trip, but that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was the route that you took, the road that you took, to Kozarac hospital, very quickly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The road leading from Banja Luka towards Kozarac, that is, the new road. And instead of turning off to Kamicani, we turned off to the old road which is also leading towards Kozarac and Prijedor on to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you reached the hospital, did you get to know as to what happened to the wounded person, the person whom you took to hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we stopped, we saw that a number of medical personnel had already gathered there, people whom I knew by sight who were staff members of this hospital. They helped us carry him out of the truck, and I handed the MAN over to them. But one of them said: "This man is finished," meaning that he had died. I must say that I was very afraid at that moment. I didn't inquire further about what happened, whether he died indeed or not. I'm just telling you this brief comment that I heard from this person. That was the first thing that I learned and the only thing that I learned about this man. After that, that is, after we took this unfortunate man out of the truck, the shelling continued, and it was getting closer to the hospital, to the area surrounding the hospital, while we were still there. At that moment, the shelling even intensified, so we had to seek shelter in the basement of this hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was the hospital building damaged? Did you see any damage caused to the hospital building by the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the shelling, that is, during the shelling, we made several attempts at leaving the basement. We wanted to continue on our way. It was impossible to see from the basement what was going on, but we could hear that the explosions were very near. The hospital itself was affected. The glass on the windows were smashed and pieces of it were falling all around the hospital, including the stairway leading down to the basement. But we managed to leave the basement at one point in time. It was a very brief lull in the shelling. When we got out, we were able to see that the truck that we had used to bring this man to the hospital had also been hit. So it was impossible for us to take the same vehicle back. So we seized this lull in the shelling, this opportune moment, and came out. I could see that everything had been badly damaged, including the hospital building, the windows on the hospital, and the truck. But we managed to leave the area and we continued on towards our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, did you get to know the name of the person, the wounded person whom you took to hospital and subsequently succumbed to injuries? Did you get to know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was a local resident from the same village as we were. His family name was Foric. I don't know what his name was, but I think he was called Ile. People called him "Ile," so his name could be Ilijaz, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How was he dressed at this time? Was he a civilian, dressed in civvies, civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing jeans, denim trousers at any rate. He had a T-shirt and a shirt on top of the T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that you returned to Kamicani.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Kamicani after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think I stayed there for about two hours. I think I was back home between 5.00 and 6.00 after I left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in Kamicani, until when -- how long were you in Kamicani after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 26th of May, the afternoon hours of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was Kamicani shelled during this period, from the 24th to the 26th? Could you very briefly explain what you observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ever since the very beginning of the shelling and my departure from that area, rounds kept falling almost all the time, but sporadically, with intervals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, 1992, did your family leave the house in Kamicani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Due to the shelling and the firing from infantry weapons which was getting closer and closer, and also because of the fact that we were able to see houses on fire from the direction of Banja Luka, we decided that the moment had come for us to leave our houses. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you say "the family," who are the people who left the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring to my immediate family and a number of neighbours who were with us at the time; specifically, people who were hiding in the basement of this house and with whom we left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you say, "hiding in the basement," they were taking refuge in the house from the shelling; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Why else would they be there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we had decided to leave our homes, we had some kind of informal conversation amongst ourselves. I mean, it happened very quickly. We decided to leave in the direction of Trnopolje, not exactly for Trnopolje, but we decided to go in that direction. I decided to go in the opposite direction and to leave for the woods because it seemed to me that because of the nature of the terrain, it would be easier for us to hide from the fighting which was getting closer. So we parted in this house. They went to the south and I went in the opposite direction, northward. After about 10 or 15 minutes of walk in the direction of these woods, I realised that I had made a mistake. I kept asking myself: "Why should I go to the area which is supposedly safer and let my family, my wife and my child, go in the opposite direction"? And it was at that moment that I decided to go back and join them, and then come what may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were any of the people --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were any of the people who were with you armed at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, there were no weapons there whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And then you said that you decided to go and look for your family. So did you proceed in search of your family and see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As I said, I was for a while walking in the opposite direction, but then I decided to go back and join them. While still on the road, I saw a truck which was parked in the vicinity of my house. This house was the property of my company, and I decided to take this truck and to follow them, to try to get to them as quickly as possible. And I was moving in the opposite direction of the attack. As I was driving through the village, trying to get to my family and other people, I saw that the place had already been abandoned by its residents. I didn't see anyone inside or outside their houses. Of course, I couldn't see inside. But I didn't see anyone around. I kept looking to the left, hoping to see them. I wanted to give them a sign so that they know that I was following them, that I was with this truck which I thought could take us from the area much faster, take us out of the area much faster. I probably drove very fast -- actually, I know I did. And looking to the right and to the left, more to the left, I came across a military vehicle, a pinzgauer, which was covered with a canvas and was carrying a number of armed soldiers who were sitting on both sides of the truck. The vehicle was moving in the same direction as my truck and I caught them -- and I caught up with them. At that moment, they stopped and they pointed their rifles at me. So I had to stop and get out of the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, these soldiers, did you recognise them? Were they Serb soldiers? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers were wearing the usual Yugoslav military uniform, the one I was familiar with, but they had no insignia on. They had helmets on their heads, but the helmets did not have the usual five-pointed star, which must have been covered with some black scotch tape. One of them had a cap, the usual Yugoslav army cap, with the five-pointed red star.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you beaten and questioned, or questioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't beat me. The first thing they told me was to curse me. They verbally abused me, started calling me names, and they shouted at me, telling me to discard my weapon, but it was obvious that I didn't have any weapon. They said: "Drop that weapon." But I said: "You can see that I don't have any." So they continued with a number of questions. They wanted to know where I was going, what I was up to, and I told them. I told them what my intentions were. This lasted for a while. We talked, but all the time they had their rifles pointed at me. I told them that I went to search for my family, that I wanted to save my family, but that I was not sure that I would be able to do that. One of them, the one with the cap with the five-pointed star, came closer and addressed me in a somewhat calmer way. And he asked me once again where I was going, and I told him again what I had already told them. At that moment while we were talking, the family, that is, the people, were passing by. They were behind their backs. And I showed them -- I pointed to those people, trying to explain to them what I was about to do. So they turned around, and some of them, my father, my mother, and some elderly people who were not moving very fast, who could not walk as quickly as the younger ones who had already left, turned around. And they said that they should board the truck. A number of other residents came out of the shelters, and they were all put on this truck, which I then drove in the direction of Kozarac, that is, towards -- to the T junction leading to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You drove the truck with the others who were put on to your truck. Was any other truck escorting you, escorting the truck that was driven by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. The soldiers who were with their vehicle, they were driving the same direction. I don't remember whether they were ahead of me or behind me because at that moment while this was going on, while people were being loaded on to the truck, a number of other residents showed up driving tractors, people who had gathered from the surrounding houses who all formed a kind of small convoy which included this military vehicle carrying Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you all ultimately taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ultimately, we were taken to the school building in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you say "the school building in Trnopolje," could you describe very briefly what this place was? And this was on the 26th of May, 1992; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct. This lasted for a while. I just told you the end of the story. The event happened on the 26th of May but late at night, between 10.00 and 11.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you describe the place, the school building, and the other buildings around in Trnopolje, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It consisted of a school building, an elementary school building, a shop, football pitch, and a building which housed the local community centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was there a cinema, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a cinema hall there, but I don't think that it worked regularly. It was part of the community centre which had -- which organised various types of activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What you referred as "local community centre" was the cinema that I referred to; am I correct? That was a big hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you reached Trnopolje, what did you observe there other than the buildings that you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We reached Trnopolje at night. I drove in, into the compound, between the building that we referred to a moment ago, that is, the community centre building, the cinema hall, and the shop. It was dark. The buses carrying women, children, and men followed my truck into the compound, and we stopped there. I didn't actually enter the school compound. And at that moment, I was not aware of what was going on in the school building or who was there. I was still outside. After a while, the buses were emptied, and I lingered on for some time. A number of other buses and trucks arrived in the meantime, and that's how I spent the night, out in the open. On the following day, when it became light, I saw for the first time that people were actually sleeping out in the open, in the school yard. There were many people there, including a number of children who were crying. I also noticed that the school was also packed, including the school yard. But we were still standing outside at that time. Most of the people there were residents of neighbouring communities such as Kozarac and Kamicani, and I knew most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, did you observe anybody in control or in authority other than the people who had come there from the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I didn't make any decisions or choices as to the route we were supposed to take. It was the soldiers who told us where to go, where to turn at various junctions such as Kozarac. There were armed soldiers posted everywhere, so they were the ones who led us towards Trnopolje. So the next day, when we arrived, when it dawned, I realised where we were. We could still hear shooting and firing coming from various directions, and I saw the next day that there were quite a few people in military uniforms around this place. So there we were, and I realised that it was not possible for us to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: At that time in the camp, did you learn who was in charge of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The camp commander was a major by the name of Slobodan Kuruzovic. He was the camp commander throughout the period of time while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were there guards in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course, the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a convenient moment to take a break, the adjournment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Apologies for being late due to problems in another case. I heard that there would be an issue to be raised as regards signatures. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As Your Honour knows, an issue that the Court, the Trial Chamber, has identified as a key issue in this case is the signatures on many of the documents issued by -- or that have been presented by the Office of the Prosecutor, and in particular, documents that we contend were signed by Dr. Stakic. Most of the documents in dispute, the Defence has admitted that Dr. Stakic authored three documents that were signed in Cyrillic. Most of those that are in dispute are signatures that appear to me to be in Latin and signed "S. Milomir," and I believe the Defence objected to those and raised the issue, I believe Mr. Lukic said it was highly questionable that a document would be signed with the first name of someone who was the president of a municipality or Crisis Staff. We asked Your Honours for an order to seize the documents that were written by the accused since his detention in the custody of the Detention Unit and also documents that he had on him at the time of the arrest, and Your Honours were kind enough to grant that order on the 5th of July, I believe. The order specifically excluded material in the cell of the accused. When we asked for this order, we were aware that Dr. Stakic had certain documents in his possession at the time of his arrest that were turned over by the Office of the Prosecutor to the Registrar. When we got back the material from Judge Lindholm, those documents were not included. And I had asked my investigators to track those down, and I received the information this morning that apparently the documents were photocopied by the OTP, and then handed over to the OLAD unit. We received information from Melinda Taylor today that those documents had been given to the Detention Unit and that the Detention Unit reported to her this morning that there's a note on the file indicating that, except for certain passports and I believe a driver's license that was retained, all other documents were turned over to the accused, and they believe that they are in his cell. I think that's speculation, but they were turned over to the accused since his detention, and he hasn't been released since that time. Directing Your Honours' attention, for example, to the documents in front of you, the page -- I am just going to use the ERN stamp on the top, the page that ends with the numbers 204. I believe this has to do, this document, with a customs violation or customs something, kind of a demand from the customs unit in Yugoslavia or Serbia. And there's a signature on the bottom right which I believe appears to be the same as the signatures on many of the Crisis Staff documents. Going to page 205, which appears to be something to do with an airline ticket, on the bottom left, there's a signature that appears to me to be S. Milomir. Going to page 208, there are two receipts for rent, and the signature of the rentor on the bottom left of each of the documents appears to be the same signature that is disputed on the Crisis Staff documents, S. Milomir. Going to page 209, there is another document from Luka Beograd. And again, the signature under the words "primio" appears to be similar to the S. Milomir signatures in dispute. And the very last page, on page 721, you see under "primio" the S. Milomir signature. These, I think, are highly relevant in that they were on the accused at the time of his arrest. I don't believe under my domestic -- my experience in domestic jurisdiction, or any jurisdiction, a person in a detention unit has an expectation of privacy as to their documents in a cell, otherwise, there wouldn't be security in those units. I have two alternative requests: One is that the Defence agrees - which of course they do not have to and it should not be held against them - to provide these documents, or secondly that Your Honour order the Detention Unit to go -- we can give them an exact copy of the documents we're looking for, to look in his cell and see if they can find these documents, the reason being although the handwriting experts will get some use from the photocopies, it is much, much preferable to them to have the original signatures, which I'm not sure -- I have to admit I'm not sure that the documents that we're talking about are "original" originals, whether Dr. Stakic had photocopies in his possession or had originals in his possession. That I'm not sure of because I haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt that a forensic handwriting expert needs originals, not photocopies. But if I understand correctly, the documents were handed over to the OTP, and then photocopies were taken, and the originals given back?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That is what I found out, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It seems not to be professional. But we have to resolve this issue. Of course, there is no obligation, but I remember when there was a review whether or not the documents were privileged or not, Mr. Lukic was present. Probably, he can, if he so wants only, to help us out whether there were originals or only photocopies. You can discuss this, of course, and ever before answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I'd like to address that point because I spoke to Mr. Koumjian from the OTP in connection with these documents, and perhaps he can clarify further. These were not documents that the Defence had in its possession or were transmitted to the OTP during or subsequent to the Court's order. So -- and I just wanted clarification on that, and I think Mr. Koumjian is nodding, but I would rather have it on the record. These are documents that were provided, in our opinion, and I have an objection to it specifically, ex parte without the Defence or the Defence lawyers at any time having any knowledge or any information about these documents. They were held in abeyance from us at all times until now, this morning, when they were tendered to us, apparently when they were again reviewed by Mr. Koumjian and his team of investigators. So if the Court's question is whether we were present when Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. originals were photocopied and given to the OTP, I think Mr. Koumjian can answer that, and the answer is an unequivocal "no." Because today is the first time that we received a copy of these documents and I've never seen the original in any form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the Defence can only act as one act, and it should be relatively easy for Mr. Lukic, having been present during the review, to identify whether or not these documents were in the envelope received from the Detention Unit and opened in his presence by Judge Lindholm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, these documents were not in the envelope which was opened in my presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This means that there is an additional request by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I understand it, a request for a search and seizure order as regards the cell unit of Dr. Stakic limited to the originals of the documents we have in photocopy before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Exactly correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 11.30. --- Break taken at 11.16 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. The Defence has heard the request by the Office of the Prosecutor. You have, of course, now the right to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With respect to this request, we would like initially for the record to state that we would incorporate our arguments that we had set forth for the Court initially during the initial request for the subpoena, and for the same bases as I've outlined at that time, we think the request should, or the supplemental request, should likewise be denied. In addition, however, we think there are two additional relevant and important matters that need to be addressed with respect to this additional supplemental request. First, we think that this request is far beyond the parameters of relevance and necessity. The OTP has not only the burden of proof in this case, as we've outlined, but on each and every issue, we believe they are required to set forth at least the prima facie basis as to why those documents are reasonable. By merely stating that they had the documents in their possession, had them photocopied, and never gave it to the Defence at any time, although we believe the Rules specifically would have allowed and directed them to provide us with copies of those documents throughout the proceedings, but most specifically at the time when this issue was raised, the OTP should have immediately put us on notice, should have immediately given us copies of those documents, and we would have immediately - as opposed to now within the last 10 or so minutes - consulted with our client in connection with those issues. We have been denied that. We have been denied, in essence, a fair proceeding, in our opinion respectfully. In addition to that, we think what the OTP is, in reality, doing is trying to change the law of the appellate court that was cited during our earlier objection regarding handwriting samples. It's one thing to take the position to suggest - and the case is obviously the Delalic case in Celebici - is to ask the Court for a handwriting sample which is specifically prohibited. But does it really not equate to the same thing, as opposed to asking an accused for handwriting samples, the OTP in every case merely waits in the bushes, allows the accused to write letters to his family, correspond with his counsel, correspond with other members or friends in the community, and then in the middle of the trial ask for those samples of handwriting. The OTP knew which elements were required in this case from the outset, as set forth in their pretrial brief that they filed months before the trial commenced. We believe that this is an attempt to override and an attempt through the back door to circumvent the decisional authority that has been decided by the appellate chamber and that this Court, we believe, has followed rather closely. For those two reasons, Your Honour, we ask that their motion to supplement these documents be summarily denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admittedly, the Trial Chamber was surprised by this request, but the request seems to be only consequent and we have to take care that we do the necessary without violating the principle of proportionality. Therefore, for the reasons given in our decision of 5 July, 2002 and taking into account the arguments given by the OTP and by the Defence today, the Trial Chamber orders that, only for the purpose of finding the originals of the documents handed over to us some minutes ago, a search in the cell unit of Dr. Stakic should be executed. But this should not be executed before Dr. Stakic returns to the cell unit, but on the other hand, Dr. Stakic will be not allowed to enter the cell unit before this enforcement of this order can take place. The search should take place, or has to take place, in the presence of a witness of the United Nations Detention Unit, and it should be executed, as mentioned beforehand, immediately, and it's restricted only to finding the originals of these documents. Having found these documents, once again, the documents should be put into an envelope. This envelope has to be sealed. And then in analogy, the procedure has to follow as it was set out in our decision of 5 July 2002, and the review should be conducted by Judge Per Lindholm in the presence of counsel for Dr. Stakic. We believe that the Prosecutor, by showing us the examples, has established that it is necessary to have these documents in the original version. And as regards the opinion of the Defence, it is, of course, not to take handwriting samples; it is to take documents which were, for totally different reasons, were produced in the past. And we already, when discussing the draft for the decision of 5 July 2002, we balanced the interests of the parties and came to the conclusion that, indeed, there would be no obstacle to obtain such documents not prepared for the purpose of getting here during trial new handwriting samples. Therefore, we expect that the OTP is able to conduct this exercise today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, obviously, that's necessary. Would Your Honour like me to mark as an exhibit these eight pages that I've shown Your Honour? And I think the record might be clearer if they were made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For these purposes, but only for these purposes, I think it's necessary to have these eight pages as -- marked as exhibits. Objections by the Defence? It's now on the photocopies we have before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, there's no objection to proceeding in marking those eight pages as Mr. Koumjian does direct. I do have a practical issue with the Court's order, if I may address with the Court at this time respectfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We recognise and understand Your Honours' ruling. Respectfully, we disagree with it. However, my practical problem with respectfully disagreeing with the Court is that our rights to proceed with a potential appeal have to be discussed, digested, possibly debated between the client and the team involved. We think, if the Court would be kind enough to modify its order to - and I understand the urgency from the Court's point of view, again respectfully disagreeing with it - to have this seizure take place, but that the documents do not be tendered to the OTP for examination until we have come to a conclusion under our rights under the Rules within seven days to ask for an interlocutory appeal on this issue. It's not a delay. We're not asking the Court to in any way interfere with the logic that has been shared with us in the decision. However, we think we still have some rights and would like to determine whether or not we would exercise those rights in a timely fashion. So what I would propose, if I may, is that if the Court orders the seizure, that the documents be kept in the possession and retention of an authorised person, such as a member of the Detention Unit, today, from what I can understand from the Court's ruling, and give us an opportunity to respond as to what, if any, objection we have as to proceeding with the next step, i.e. presenting it to the judge and then having the OTP and the Defence counsel examine that together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me address this immediately because it has already been resolved, this problem. Please find in our decision, and I said it had to be applied analogously. In the end, when it comes how to enforce a decision, we stated that all remedies available under the Rules remain untouched. And for the purposes of today's search and seizure, this does mean, in the light of what we heard now, that the sealed envelope has to be given immediately to Judge Lindholm and will not be opened before you had the right under the Rules to ask for certification for an appeal. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's turn to the documents. The former -- the document with the number ending with 203, 204 will be S220. 205 will be S221. Is it correct that there is no 206, 207?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then 208, S222. 209, 223. 212, S224. Ending with 198, S225. Ending with 721, S226.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that the number on the photocopy is cut off. I believe that's 7211, that last document, because there should be eight digits in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, right. But you agree, we can't read it from the document, so the ending number is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to explain to the Defence what I think the answer is, these numbers are not -- there are some numbers like 206 and 207 that are missing because this is a selection of the ones that we thought contained the signatures we were interested in. So if Mr. Ostojic or Mr. Lukic wants the other documents, they can be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I expect the necessary to be done and the Detention Unit to be informed beforehand that the procedure can be executed as expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could be excused to try to arrange this, this afternoon. Mr. Waidyaratne will carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then may the witness, if there are no other issues -- but please bring the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The only other issue is we will take the OTP's offer on providing us with a complete set of documents that are in their possession that they took from our client. So that would be nice. Even though we are close to the end of their case, we would appreciate it in any event. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's fair enough, and it was offered. Do you think you can finalise within the next 90 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I think probably, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we give you the necessary leeway, having had now a longer and short break. But in order to come to a conclusion, please proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I would. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, our apologies for this unforeseeable interruption of your examination. It will now proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I at this stage ask for private session, Your Honour. There may be some answers that he will touch upon some personal identification. So, therefore, may I request a private session at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, you said that even the local mosque was destroyed or damaged. Did you see the local mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did because we had to pass by the local mosque on our way to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mosque had also been set on fire. There were no longer any door frames or window frames on it. The minaret was down. It had collapsed, I think to the west. That is how we found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: This is the mosque in Kamicani. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, how long did you stay in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until they closed down the camp, that is, until the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How did you get your food during the time that you spent in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, there was a Red Cross vehicle, just an ordinary vehicle, which was used by the people, that is, the employees of the local Red Cross. Those people were from Prijedor. Which vehicle was used by them to bring bread, and we would form a line when this truck arrived and each of us could get two slices of bread. This lasted only for a while at the very beginning. And soon after, the population of the neighbouring houses, that is, the people who lived in the vicinity, mostly women, started bringing us food. So while these people were still there, it was possible for us to get some food from them, from acquaintances or relatives, depending on who you knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you provided with medical facilities, medicines, during the time that you spent in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a few doctors there, Bosniaks, who had been given a room which was in the local commune building in Trnopolje. And detainees could go to them for help. I don't know what problems other people had. I myself suffered from kidney pain. I must have had some kind of inflammation, and I did go to see these people, these doctors. They told me that they knew what it was but they couldn't do anything to help me. They didn't have any medical supplies. But they told me that my condition was not a life-threatening one, and they gave me some other medicine, the one that they had -- the only one they could give me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, did you see people with injuries or any beatings that took place in the camp, while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. During my stay there, which was not a short one, from the beginning until the end, people were taken out for interrogation and then taken back. When I say "interrogation," that is what they -- that is what they called it. I don't know what they did with them. But very often, they would come back badly beaten and covered with blood. I don't know what questions had been asked of them but they often came back injured, with wounds that had to be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any person die or being killed in the camp? I may say "die" in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the camp proper, I did see one person die. And I heard -- I was informed that many people did die indeed, but I did see this one person whose name I did not know. That was midway through my stay in the camp. People were being brought in from the surroundings of Prijedor, Hambarine, and those villages over there. We were sleeping Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. outside, so those people, too, were next to where I was in the camp. This was an elderly man. I'm not sure what the reason was but he had to use the toilet all the time. So this went on like that for two or three days, and that's where he then died. Perhaps dysentery or something like that. That's what I heard had been the cause of his death, but no one can say really, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was he provided with any medical assistance or medicines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man was there next to me, and I never saw any doctors attending his illness. And perhaps had he been given the proper medicines, he would not have died.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a convenient moment to break, or I would go on for another 10 or 15 minutes if it's okay, permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Then I would be able to conclude my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any persons being called out and taken out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. During my stay in the camp, I was an eyewitness to several occasions where police officers, Serb police officers, would enter the camp. Two of them, they stood there at the perimeter for a while, for perhaps 15 or 20 minutes, looking completely disinterested. After a while, they approached a group of persons who were sleeping, quite literally, next to an outbuilding. One of the group approached them in turn, a man I knew, and then one of the police officers offered him a cigarette. He lit the cigarette. I did not even overhear their conversation, but judging by their gestures, I had the impression that they were acquaintances. Perhaps if they had something against that man, they wouldn't have offered him the cigarette. Maybe they would have beaten him. That was my impression. So while he was still smoking, he went back to where he had come from, and then he returned again with another five people, so there were six of them. And at one point, they all began talking to one another. And after a brief conversation, they moved and went behind the building that we had earlier described as the cinema. Once they reached the corner of that building, I saw that the six of them had their hands behind their heads, and they moved towards the exit of the camp. And at that moment, my impression was that the scene was strange, and other people who watched this said the same because the conversation at first seemed friendly. But then they were made to put their hands behind their heads when they reached the corner of the house. And then 15, 20 minutes, perhaps half an hour later, we heard sounds of shooting from semi-automatic weapons. Shots were fired. I did not see this but I heard those shots. And after the initial barrage, there were individual shots, and I could count them. I could discern them clearly. There were six shots being fired. But even at that point, I could not know exactly what had happened. After a few days, a group of people from the camp went to bury the bodies of those six people, which probably implied that they had on that occasion been killed behind that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you -- you said that you knew the man who was given the cigarette. Do you remember the name of the person? Do you recall the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. His name was Zilhad Foric

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you recognise any others with him who were taken with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. His brother, whose name I don't know; his two neighbours, also by the last name of Foric. So I can remember their father's name but I can't give you their names now. I know the name of one of their brothers who is still alive but, well, you see, I can't remember now. And there were another two persons. They were also brothers. I did not know them, but they came from the same village of Forici. So there were three couples of brothers who had been taken off. And then the other two persons whose names I didn't know, their father's name was Rasim. And one of these persons was called Zihad, and the other I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The six people with the last name Foric, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, when you were in the camp, were you able to move out and into the camp freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Move in and out freely, no, we were not allowed to. But we drank the water we got from across the way from where the camp was because there was no drinking water inside the camp. So we had to queue up, normally. And guards at the checkpoint where we were crossing the road would let us cross two by two to go and fetch the water. So we took turns two by two. That was the moment when you could actually leave the camp. As early as August, I think it was late August when those water supplies that we were using were practically exhausted, and those women could no longer bring us food in the camp because they had been expelled from the area and no longer lived in the surroundings. Whenever the guards were well disposed, they would allow us to go and forage for food in the surrounding houses, whatever food was still there left behind for us to eat. So these were the only opportunities we got to actually leave the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Just briefly before we end, what about the women and the females that were in the camp? Did you see them being harassed or being taken out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Women in the camp. From the very beginning to, I believe, the month of August, women, but not only women, also children, were brought in, women and children who had been expelled from the surrounding villages. They would usually put them up in the cinema hall and part of the area behind the camp. Sometimes they would stay for three, five, seven days, and then they would be transported further by rail and taken off somewhere. We did not know where these women and children were being taken. As far as harassment of women is concerned, during my stay, I did not notice any such cases. But one particular night, when there were people inside the camp who had come from outside, from the surrounding area, supposedly soldiers arrived in the camp who were not camp guards but members of some combat unit who were doing, well, I guess only they knew what, in the Kozarac area. They came during the night, and they would take off women and girls and take these women and girls along with them, some of whom were returned the following day, and some even later. I should suppose that they had been raped. My only knowledge of that was that the following day, the camp commander himself was in the camp - that was Kuruzovic - and he was surrounded by a group of women. I approached them as their conversation was ending, and I only heard him say the following. He said: "I'll look into this matter. This must not happen again." And of course I asked the women what they were talking about. And those were mothers and sisters who had been taken off to be raped, and they complained to him while they were still inside the camp. And I thought this was a brave gesture on their part to approach him and ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, you left Trnopolje on the 1st of October, 1992. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The trial stays adjourned until 5 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Witness U, for the purposes of a fairly conducted trial, it's now for the Defence to put forward to you some additional questions. And please answer them in the same way you did as vis-a-vis the Prosecutor. Thank you for your understanding. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness U. My name is John Ostojic, and along with Branko Lukic, we represent Dr. Milomir Stakic. I will be asking you a series of questions here this afternoon, as the Court has informed you, and I appreciate your candor in responding to them. You are still under oath, sir. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, in the village and area of which you grew up and came, whether anyone else shared the same last name and first name other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you want to go in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Usher may take away the list, please. Take away the list, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, earlier today, you testified about various checkpoints that inhibited you from going to the Prijedor area, if you recall. My question to you, sir: Prior to April of 1992, were you aware of any Muslim checkpoints that were put up in any part of the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prior to April, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about during the month of April 1992, sir, were you aware of any checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Kozarac area, the TO was active, and I think that in May checkpoints were set up in Kozarac itself. Not only do I think so but I know it for a fact. That's the road into Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss May in a moment, but with respect to April, are you familiar whether or not the Territorial Defence, as you've identified them in your previous answer, in Kozarac actually developed any or had any checkpoints in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't say with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, there is a disagreement with respect to the interpretation of the answer provided on line 18 of page 63 of this witness's prior statement. And perhaps we could assist by sharing with the Court and the interpreter what we believe the witness said and how it was interpreted. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate if you put the same question once more briefly to the witness, and then let's see how the translation will read.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness U, is it your testimony that you cannot say positively or negatively whether or not there were Muslim checkpoints set up in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't answer. It's not that I can't answer, I do not know in that sense. The answer is neither yes nor no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, turning to May of 1992, I think you stated that you knew or you knew for a fact that there were checkpoints in the Kozarac area. How did you, sir, come to know that there were checkpoints that were manned exclusively by the Muslim residents or the Muslims of the Territorial Defence in Kozarac in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I -- to clarify a point whether the witness said that there were exclusively Muslim checkpoints, I don't see any reference to Muslim checkpoints, neither in the answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Fair enough. Please rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in May of 1992 in the Kozarac area, how many checkpoints were you aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the road when you leave Kozarac, that is, the approach road leading up to the main road, Prijedor/Banja Luka Road, not far from the sawmill, some 200 metres away, thereabouts. But this was in May, sometime in May prior to the events which took place as of the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to the 24th of May in due course. But prior to that, the checkpoint that you were familiar with, sir, can you identify for us by whom was it manned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The control was carried out by the members of the Prijedor Territorial Defence, that is, the people from the area of Kozarac who were officially members of the Prijedor Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me understand this, sir: Is it your testimony that there was a separate Territorial Defence known as the TO of Kozarac and then yet another Territorial Defence identified as the Territorial Defence of Prijedor within that time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is that the Territorial Defence, that is, when I speak about the Territorial Defence, I am referring to the people, member of the reserve force of the Yugoslav army and who were active in the area of Kozarac and whose command was located somewhere in the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup of those people within that Territorial Defence organisation that you're referencing, sir, that was at the checkpoint near the road exiting Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The makeup of the Territorial Defence, as far as the people whom I knew are concerned, was mixed, people from various ethnic groups, including Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you not say "the majority of which were Muslims"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're having a little trouble with respect to the interpretation, and I thought you said that. When you say "majority were Muslims," sir, of that checkpoint, can you quantify that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may have been a misunderstanding. I was referring to the members of the Territorial Defence whom I knew in Kozarac. Specifically as regards this checkpoint, I wasn't referring to this very checkpoint a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's take it one step at a time, if we may. With respect to the members of the Territorial Defence that you were aware of, I believe it's your testimony that the majority of them were Muslims. Can you quantify that amount for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards my assessment of the actual number, I don't want to make a mistake. I can only speak about the people whom I knew personally, people who were members of the civilian Territorial Defence. As for the overall composition of the force, I cannot say anything. I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what other ethnic groups were members of this civil Territorial Defence that you reference in which you had known the majority of Muslims made the composition of such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So your question is who else was there, apart from Muslims, members of which other ethnic groups, as far as I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like I said, all of them were there, I mean all -- there were people whom I knew by name and surname who were members of this Territorial Defence and were of Serb ethnicity whom I would see from time to time in uniforms of the Territorial Defence. But as regards the actual number, I cannot tell you much about that. I can only speak about some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just a couple questions if I may, in light of the time, ask on this point, sir. Is it your testimony that in May of 1992, the Territorial Defence was composed of both Muslim, Serb, and Croatian groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May, I don't know what the makeup was in the end but the Territorial Defence was of mixed nature, of mixed character. When we talk about various formations, there were people from various ethnic groups who were members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if this is a good time to break in light of the time. I think we're only allowed the courtroom until 1.45. I obviously have more, and I may take another hour and-a-half to two hours, Your Honour, just to let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the light of this, indeed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My apologies. It's necessary to have a break now, and we continue then for another line of questions. Apparently you said one and-a-half to two hours tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this concludes the 54th day of the hearing. And I may ask the witness to come back tomorrow for additional questions, both by the Defence and probably additional questions by the Judges. Thank you for assisting us today. And resume tomorrow, 9.00 -- sorry, tomorrow in the afternoon at 14.15, and the courtroom will be Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 1.47 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of July, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
